newsitem.title: UK: Greenspan speech fixates world markets.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan speech fixates world markets.

text.p: Three months after Federal Reserve chief Alan Greenspan sent global markets into a spin by warning against "irrational" stock market gains, markets were on Tuesday braced for his next setpiece speech on the state of the economy.

With some economists cautioning that strength in the U.S. labour market could raise inflation risks later this year, his address to U.S. legislators gives him an opportunity to set out any concerns on economic trends and flag any change of policy.

Greenspan's prime responsibility remains the health of the domestic economy, yet his words will be scrutinised around the world for hints and nuances about the evolution of policy in the world's biggest economy.

And with Wall Street riding high at near-record levels -- in turn helping boost stock markets around the world -- equities could prove particularly sensitive to any suggestion that Fed interest rate policy is poised to change course.
Analysts on Tuesday said they expected some cautionary words from Greenspan, aimed primarily at once again demonstrating his reputation for monetary responsibility.

"There are worries that Greenspan may make strong statements about speculation in the market, about tightness in labour markets and upward pressure on wages," said Hugh Johnson, chief strategist at First Albany Corp. in the United States.
"But it's not so much an issue of what he says as the passion he says it with."
An avowed anti-inflation hawk, the 70-year old central banker has cemented his reputation for financial rectitude during nearly 10 years as head of the world's most powerful financial institution.
A master at portraying a cautious and responsible approach to monetary policy, his tenure has nonetheless frequently been controversial.
Through 1994 he progressively tightened monetary policy to ward off a perceived inflation risk, weighing on stocks and bonds through the year.

Last December he again showed why markets cannot afford to ignore his words, when his by-now familiar warning against "irrational exuberance" in financial markets sent the Dow, treasury bonds -- and stocks and bonds around the world -- into a tailspin albeit short-lived.
Yet since Greenspan's December comments, reflecting fears that an overvalued Wall Street may itself pose inflation risks, the Dow has risen over 500 points to set new highs above the 7,000 level.

Economists said the key risk for markets this time is that Greenspan's so-called "Humphrey Hawkins" testimony on Wednesday will sound a warning over the possibility that rising labour market pressures could pose an inflation risk later this year.
"Financial markets can anticipate some cautioning remarks," said Salomon Brothers economist Bob DiClemente.
"Despite continuing favourable inflation news, policy remains poised to respond to possible price pressures."
At Merrill Lynch, economist Bruce Steinberg also said markets should be on alert for hints of inflation concerns, though he expects no imminent rate rise.

"My guess is that Greenspan will sound somewhat hawkish, again warning about incipient wage pressures," said Steinberg in a research note. "His remarks may well disturb the bond and equity markets. Yet I believe that the Fed is in no hurry to tighten policy."
Yet another possibility is that the real risks on the U.S. economy are already well known and Greenspan will deliver little of fresh interest for the markets.
"There has been so much talk about the Fed's position," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase Manhattan in London. "It could be a bit of a non-event."
